ELI5: How does presidential elections work in the United States?

In the final presidential election there are actually more than two parties running, although if you vote for one other than republican or democrat you are basically throwing away your vote because the other parties get far less votes and cannot raise the money for campaigning.

Bernie Sanders was independent but he recently announced he is running for the democratic party for president. This is probably because it would be almost impossible for him to win independently. So he is now in a race against Hillary (and any other democratic candidates) to be nominated by the democratic party to run as their presidential candidate. This nomination is determined by a primary election, where members of the democratic party from each state will vote on which candidate it wants to run for the democratic party.

1) Candidates for the different parties are chosen by voters during caucus elections. For example you'll have a vote for the democratic nominee, a vote for the republican nominee, and so on (Green Party, etc. independents are, well, independent so this step does not concern them).

2) The winners of these caucus votes choose their running mate. (This is would be their Vice President).

3) The election. Each state (Aside from Nebraska and Maine I believe) have an election where if the majority vote for a party, that party nominee takes that state. Each state has a certain number of votes (based on population) in the Electoral College. The electoral college is the one who ultimately makes the vote for president. When a party wins a state, those votes for that party are used to vote for the respective nominee via the electoral college. It's like the electoral college votes on the states' behalf. The electoral college is not necessarily required to vote with what the state is supposed to vote as, but it is very unlikely they will vote against the states.

It's all quite a process. Personally, I'll never quite understand why there is still an electoral college. If someone could explain that to me, I'd appreciate it.
This might make it a little clearer for you

Okay, there are two things you need to understand about Presidential Elections first:

  1. The General Election (i.e. the one in November) is the only one governed by the Constitution; the Primaries are entirely up to the discretion of their parties. They still have to obey certain campaign laws, but every political party can decide pick its candidate in any manner it chooses.

  2. When we vote for President the US, we're not actually voting for the candidate themselves. In the primaries (which is what we're getting ready for now), we're voting for delegates that will go to the convention and nominate our candidate. In the general election, we're voting for "Electors" who then go on and elect the President and Vice President.

Now, for your question.

I keep reading Bernie Senders is an independent, but he is now in a race with Hillary Clinton(?) So is he a democrat?

Bernie Sanders is running for the Democratic Nomination because he knows that: A) that's his best chance for victory, and B) he met the filing requirements of the Party. Since the Parties are free to set their own rules for selecting a candidate, they're free to pick anyone they choose... even if the person isn't "technically" a Democrat.

 

Couldn't there be an election between him, and Hillary only? Or he, her, and another Republican?

Bernie Sanders is likely to be the nominee for one, or more, political parties. See, even though Republicans and Democrats get all the press, they're not the only political parties we have- there are dozens, and as long as their candidates have met the Federal requirements, they'll be on the ballot also. This means that, even if Bernie Sanders loses the nomination for the Democrats (which is more than likely the case) people will still be able to vote for him in November. Not good news if you're a Democrat.
